intro.en: Essential named surgical operations, clinical indications, operative steps in outline, surgical anatomy landmarks, complications, and viva voce spotter questions for final-year MBBS candidates.

items.summary: Surgical excision of the inflamed vermiform appendix through a McBurney gridiron or Lanz incision in the right iliac fossa.

blocks.title: Indications and incisions
bullets: Indicated for acute appendicitis, recurrent appendicitis, appendicular abscess (interval appendicectomy), and mucocele.
McBurney gridiron incision: oblique incision centered at McBurney point perpendicular to the spinoumbilical line.
Lanz incision: transverse skin crease incision placed 2 cm below the umbilicus centered on the mid-clavicular line (superior cosmesis).
Rutherford Morison muscle-cutting incision: extended laterally when dealing with a difficult high retrocaecal appendix.

blocks.title: Key operative steps in outline
bullets: Skin and subcutaneous tissues incised; external oblique aponeurosis split along the direction of its fibres.
Internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles separated bluntly in the line of their fibres; peritoneum picked up and incised.
Deliver the caecum by tracing the anterior longitudinal taenia coli inferiorly to the true base of the appendix.
Mesoappendix clamped, divided, and ligated, securing the appendicular artery within its free fold.
Base of the appendix crushed with artery forceps 5 mm from caecum, ligated with absorbable suture, and transected.
Stump invaginated into the caecal wall with a purse-string or Z-stitch, followed by layer-by-layer closure of the wound.

blocks.title: Complications and surgical pearls
bullets: Wound infection (surgical site infection) is the most frequent complication, especially in perforated appendicitis.
Pelvic or subhepatic abscess formation, faecal fistula from stump blow-out, and adhesive small bowel obstruction.
Always inspect the terminal 60 cm (2 feet) of ileum for Meckel diverticulum if the appendix appears normal on exploration.

viva.q: What is McBurney point and what does it represent anatomically?
viva.a: A point at the junction of the lateral third and medial two-thirds of the line joining the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus, marking the base of the appendix.

viva.q: How is the base of the vermiform appendix located intraoperatively?
viva.a: By identifying the caecum and tracing the three longitudinal taeniae coli (especially the anterior taenia libera) downwards to their confluence at the appendiceal base.

viva.q: What must you examine if the appendix is found to be macroscopically normal at laparotomy?
viva.a: Trace the terminal ileum proximally for 100 cm to exclude Meckel diverticulitis, mesenteric lymphadenitis, terminal ileitis (Crohn disease), and examine pelvic organs in females.

image.brief: Operative field illustration of an open appendicectomy showing the caecal pole delivered through a McBurney incision with mesoappendix clamped and base ligated.

items.summary: Minimally invasive laparoscopic removal of the vermiform appendix utilising three trocars and endoscopic instruments.

blocks.title: Indications and port placements
bullets: Indicated for acute appendicitis; particularly beneficial in young females (rules out gynaecological pathology) and obese patients.
Umbilical port (10 mm or 12 mm): camera port inserted via open Hasson or Veress technique for 30-degree laparoscope.
Suprapubic port (5 mm): placed in the midline 2 cm above the pubic symphysis for retraction.
Left iliac fossa port (5 mm or 10 mm): working port placed in the left lower quadrant along the mid-clavicular line.

blocks.title: Key operative steps in outline
bullets: Pneumoperitoneum established to 12 to 14 mmHg; patient placed in Trendelenburg position with left lateral tilt.
Diagnostic laparoscopy performed to survey the peritoneal cavity, pelvis, and ileocaecal region.
Appendix grasped at the tip and elevated; mesoappendix skeletonised and coagulated using bipolar diathermy, clips, or harmonic scalpel.
Appendicular base secured using two pre-tied endoloops (polydioxanone or polyglactin) or endoscopic linear cutter-stapler.
Appendix divided sharply between proximal and distal ties and placed into an endoscopic retrieval bag.
Specimen extracted through the umbilical or left lower port; peritoneal cavity irrigated and aspirated under vision.

blocks.title: Complications and clinical benefits
bullets: Benefits: significantly reduced surgical site infection, faster postoperative recovery, earlier return to work, and reduced pain.
Complications: intra-abdominal pelvic abscess (slightly higher than open surgery), stump leak, and trocar site herniation.
Always retrieve the specimen in an extraction bag to prevent port-site contamination and wound sepsis.

viva.q: Why is laparoscopic appendicectomy particularly advantageous in young female patients?
viva.a: It permits thorough visual inspection of the pelvis and adnexa to differentiate acute appendicitis from pelvic inflammatory disease, twisted ovarian cyst, or ruptured ectopic pregnancy.

viva.q: How is the appendicular base safely secured during laparoscopic appendicectomy?
viva.a: By applying two absorbable pre-tied endoloop ligatures (or an endoscopic linear stapler) at the base flush with the caecum, leaving a 2 mm stump.

viva.q: Why must the resected appendix always be placed into an endoscopic specimen retrieval bag?
viva.a: To prevent direct contact of the infected appendiceal mucosa with the abdominal wall during port extraction, avoiding port-site wound infection.

image.brief: Laparoscopic view showing three trocars triangulated toward the right iliac fossa with the appendix grasped and an endoloop being tightened around the appendicular base.

items.summary: Open repair of direct or indirect inguinal hernia by positioning a flat polypropylene mesh across the posterior wall without tension.

blocks.title: Indications and anaesthesia
bullets: Gold standard open operation for primary unilateral or bilateral direct and indirect inguinal hernias in adult patients.
Can be performed safely under local infiltration anaesthesia (step-by-step field block), spinal, or general anaesthesia.
Incision: transverse skin-crease incision placed 2 cm above and parallel to the medial two-thirds of the inguinal ligament.

blocks.title: Key operative steps in outline
bullets: External oblique aponeurosis opened along the line of fibres through the superficial inguinal ring, identifying the ilioinguinal nerve.
Spermatic cord mobilised from the pubic tubercle to the deep internal ring and encircled with a soft Penrose or rubber drain.
Indirect sac dissected from cord structures up to its neck at the internal ring; sac opened, contents reduced, and transfixed or invaginated.
Direct sac is plicated or inverted into the preperitoneal space with continuous absorbable suture without excision.
Polypropylene mesh (7.5 by 15 cm) tailored and anchored to the pubic tubercle, shelving edge of inguinal ligament, and conjoint tendon.
Slit created in the lateral edge of the mesh to accommodate the spermatic cord, creating a new prosthetic deep internal ring.

blocks.title: Complications and nerve preservation
bullets: Three sensory nerves must be identified and preserved: ilioinguinal, iliohypogastric, and genital branch of genitofemoral nerve.
Nerve entrapment in suture or mesh leads to chronic debilitating post-herniorrhaphy groin pain (neuralgia).
Other complications: seroma, haematoma, wound infection, ischemic orchitis, and testicular atrophy from venous thrombosis.

viva.q: What makes the Lichtenstein hernioplasty a 'tension-free' surgical repair?
viva.a: Instead of forcefully suturing attenuated tissues together under tension (like Bassini or Shouldice), a prosthetic polypropylene mesh bridges and reinforces the posterior wall defect without tension.

viva.q: Which three nerves traverse the inguinal canal and must be meticulously preserved?
viva.a: The ilioinguinal nerve (runs on the cord), iliohypogastric nerve (runs deep to external oblique above the canal), and genital branch of genitofemoral nerve (runs with cord vessels).

viva.q: How is the mesh anchored inferiorly and medially during a Lichtenstein repair?
viva.a: The mesh is secured medially over the pubic bone (overlapping the tubercle by 1.5 to 2 cm) and anchored to the shelving border of the inguinal ligament with continuous monofilament.

image.brief: Operative drawing showing the inguinal canal opened, spermatic cord elevated on a rubber sling, and a rectangular polypropylene mesh sutured over the posterior wall with cord traversing lateral slit.

items.summary: Surgical removal of the gallbladder through a right subcostal (Kocher) incision with dissection and ligation of the cystic duct and artery.

blocks.title: Indications and incision
bullets: Indicated for complicated acute cholecystitis, gallbladder perforation, suspicion of gallbladder cancer, or converted laparoscopy.
Incision: right subcostal (Kocher) incision placed two fingerbreadths (3 cm) below and parallel to the right costal margin.
Alternative incisions: right upper paramedian incision or upper midline laparotomy incision.
Retraction provided using moist abdominal packs and Deaver or Harrington liver retractors.

blocks.title: Key operative steps in outline
bullets: Adhesions between omentum, duodenum, and gallbladder divided; Hartmann pouch grasped with sponge-holding forceps for traction.
Peritoneum over Calot triangle incised, displaying the cystic duct, cystic artery, and common hepatic duct junction.
Cystic duct dissected to its junction with the common bile duct, ligated with non-absorbable silk or transfixed, and divided.
Cystic artery identified, double-ligated close to the gallbladder wall, and divided to avoid injury to the right hepatic artery.
Gallbladder dissected retrograde (from neck to fundus) out of the hepatic bed (fossa) in the subserosal plane with electrocautery.
Haemostasis achieved in the liver bed; subhepatic closed-suction tube drain placed in the Morrison pouch.

blocks.title: Anatomy of Calot triangle and complications
bullets: Boundaries of Calot triangle: cystic duct inferiorly, common hepatic duct medially, and inferior border of liver superiorly.
Cystic artery typically traverses the triangle of Calot; caterpillar turn of right hepatic artery (Moynihan hump) risks major injury.
Major complications: common bile duct injury (transection or clipping), biliary peritonitis, postoperative bile leak, and bleeding.

viva.q: What are the anatomical boundaries of the hepatobiliary triangle of Calot?
viva.a: Inferiorly by the cystic duct, medially by the common hepatic duct, and superiorly by the visceral inferior surface of the liver (segments IVb and V).

viva.q: What is the Moynihan hump (caterpillar turn) and why is it dangerous?
viva.a: A tortuous right hepatic artery looping down into Calot triangle close to the gallbladder neck, where it can be mistakenly clamped and divided as the cystic artery.

viva.q: When is the 'fundus-first' (anterograde) method of open cholecystectomy preferred?
viva.a: When severe dense inflammatory fibrosis in Calot triangle obscures ductal anatomy, making retrograde neck dissection hazardous for common bile duct injury.

image.brief: Surgical field view through a right subcostal incision showing Hartmann pouch retracted, cystic duct and cystic artery isolated within Calot triangle, and common bile duct identified.

items.summary: Minimally invasive removal of the gallbladder using four abdominal trocars and establishing the critical view of safety.

blocks.title: Indications and port geometry
bullets: Gold standard surgical procedure for symptomatic cholelithiasis, biliary colic, chronic cholecystitis, and gallstone pancreatitis.
Umbilical port (10 mm): camera port inserted via open cut-down (Hasson technique) for 30-degree laparoscope.
Epigastric port (10 mm): primary right-hand dissecting port placed 2 cm below xiphoid process angled towards gallbladder.
Right mid-clavicular subcostal port (5 mm): secondary assisting port for grasping Hartmann pouch.
Right anterior axillary port (5 mm): lateral port placed at level of umbilicus to push fundus cephalad over liver.

blocks.title: Critical View of Safety (Strasberg criteria)
bullets: Three mandatory criteria: (1) clearance of fibrofatty and fibrous tissue from the hepatocystic triangle.
(2) Dissection of the lower third of the gallbladder off the cystic plate (liver bed) to expose bare liver surface.
(3) Exactly two and only two tubular structures (cystic duct and cystic artery) seen entering the gallbladder.
Once the critical view is confirmed and verified by the surgical team, cystic duct and artery are clipped and divided.
Gallbladder dissected off the liver bed using hook diathermy; placed in an endobag and extracted via umbilical port.

blocks.title: Complications and conversion triggers
bullets: Major bile duct injury (incidence 0.3% to 0.5%): early conversion to open surgery if anatomy is unclear or bleeding occurs.
Biliary spillage from gallbladder tear: copious saline irrigation and removal of all dropped gallstones to avoid peritoneal abscesses.
Postoperative cystic duct stump blowout: causes biliary peritonitis or collection, treated with ERCP stenting or re-exploration.

viva.q: What are the three criteria of the Critical View of Safety (CVS) described by Strasberg?
viva.a: Complete clearance of fat/fibrous tissue in hepatocystic triangle, dissection of the lower third of gallbladder off the liver bed, and visualizing exactly two structures entering the gallbladder.

viva.q: What are the common indications to convert a laparoscopic cholecystectomy to an open procedure?
viva.a: Unclear biliary anatomy, severe frozen Calot triangle, uncontrolled bleeding, suspected bile duct injury, or discovery of suspected gallbladder carcinoma.

viva.q: What is Rouviere sulcus and what is its role as an anatomical landmark in laparoscopy?
viva.a: A horizontal cleft on the visceral liver surface anterior to the caudate process; safe dissection in Calot triangle must remain strictly ventral and superior to this sulcus.

image.brief: Laparoscopic intra-abdominal view demonstrating the Critical View of Safety: the lower third of the gallbladder detached from the liver bed showing only cystic duct and artery entering.

items.summary: Systematic surgical entry and exploration of the peritoneal cavity through a midline vertical incision for acute abdominal emergencies and trauma.

blocks.title: Indications and preparation
bullets: Generalised peritonitis, hollow viscus perforation, haemoperitoneum, blunt or penetrating abdominal trauma with shock.
Acute mechanical intestinal obstruction unresponsive to conservative management or with signs of strangulation.
Preoperative resuscitation: wide-bore IV lines, crystalloid resuscitation, Foley catheter, nasogastric decompression, antibiotics.
Incision: midline vertical laparotomy incision running from xiphoid process to pubic symphysis curving around the umbilicus.

blocks.title: Key operative steps in outline
bullets: Skin, subcutaneous tissues, and linea alba divided; peritoneum tented up with hemostats and incised carefully to avoid visceral injury.
Immediate suction of haemoperitoneum, bile, pus, or gastrointestinal contents; obtain fluid swab for microbiological culture.
In trauma: immediate four-quadrant abdominal packing with laparotomy sponges to arrest major haemorrhage.
Systematic exploration: inspect liver, spleen, stomach, duodenum, pancreas, mesenteric root, and pelvis.
Full small bowel run: examine the entire small intestine from the ligament of Treitz to the ileocaecal valve on both surfaces.
Perform definitive surgical procedure (e.g. Graham patch omentopexy for perforated ulcer, bowel resection, or splenectomy).
Warm normal saline peritoneal toilet (4 to 6 litres) until returns are crystal clear; closed abdominal drainage placed if indicated.

blocks.title: Abdominal closure and complications
bullets: Abdominal wall closed using mass closure technique: continuous monofilament suture (loop nylon or PDS) taking all layers except skin.
Suture-to-wound length ratio must be at least 4 to 1 with 1 cm bites placed 1 cm apart (Jenkins rule).
Damage control laparotomy (open abdomen / Bogota bag / vacuum dressing) used for lethal triad: hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy.
Complications: burst abdomen (wound dehiscence), enterocutaneous fistula, intra-abdominal collections, and incisional hernia.

viva.q: What is Jenkins rule for abdominal wall mass closure?
viva.a: The total length of the continuous suture used must be at least 4 times the length of the laparotomy incision, taking tissue bites 1 cm wide and 1 cm apart.

viva.q: What are the components of the lethal triad in exsanguinating abdominal trauma?
viva.a: Hypothermia, severe metabolic acidosis, and progressive coagulopathy; their emergence mandates immediate termination of surgery and damage control laparotomy.

viva.q: What is a Graham patch omentopexy?
viva.a: A surgical repair for perforated peptic ulcer where a vascularised pedicle of greater omentum is placed over the perforation and secured with full-thickness sutures.

image.brief: Surgical field view of an exploratory laparotomy through a midline incision with self-retaining Balfour retractor in place and surgeon performing a systematic small bowel run.

items.summary: Surgical excision of the thyroid gland through a transverse cervical collar incision with preservation of recurrent laryngeal nerves and parathyroids.

blocks.title: Indications and positioning
bullets: Indicated for thyroid malignancy, toxic multinodular goitre, Graves disease, compressive multinodular goitre, and retrosternal goitre.
Patient positioned supine with a shoulder sandbag (Barker position) providing cervical extension, head stabilized in a ring.
Incision: low transverse symmetrical collar crease incision (Kocher incision) placed 2 cm (two fingerbreadths) above the suprasternal notch.

blocks.title: Key operative steps in outline
bullets: Subplatysmal flaps raised superiorly to thyroid notch and inferiorly to suprasternal notch; anterior jugular veins preserved or ligated.
Investing deep cervical fascia divided in the midline; strap muscles (sternohyoid and sternothyroid) separated and retracted laterally.
Middle thyroid vein identified at the lateral border of the thyroid lobe, doubly ligated, and divided.
Superior thyroid pole mobilised; superior thyroid pedicle vessels ligated close to the thyroid capsule to protect the external laryngeal nerve.
Recurrent laryngeal nerve identified in the tracheo-oesophageal groove near the inferior thyroid artery and Berry ligament.
Superior and inferior parathyroid glands identified on their vascular stalks and preserved with capsule.
Berry ligament (suspensory ligament of thyroid) divided carefully; gland dissected off the trachea and excised.
Strap muscles approximated in midline; platysma closed with absorbable sutures; skin closed subcuticularly.

blocks.title: Complications and emergency airway crisis
bullets: Postoperative reactionary haemorrhage: tense haematoma deep to deep fascia compresses trachea causing acute airway asphyxia.
Immediate emergency intervention for haematoma: bedside opening of the wound and release of sutures; NEVER wait for theatre.
Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury causes adduction of vocal cords and acute stridor, requiring emergency tracheostomy.
Hypocalcaemic tetany from transient or permanent hypoparathyroidism presents with Chvostek and Trousseau signs.

viva.q: What is the emergency management of a tense neck haematoma after thyroidectomy?
viva.a: Immediate bedside opening of the entire wound, cutting all skin and deep fascial sutures with scissors to evacuate blood clots and relieve fatal tracheal compression.

viva.q: How is the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve protected during thyroidectomy?
viva.a: By ligating and dividing the branches of the superior thyroid vessels individually right on the thyroid capsule at the apex of the superior pole.

viva.q: What anatomical landmarks help locate the recurrent laryngeal nerve during thyroid surgery?
viva.a: The tracheo-oesophageal groove, Simon triangle (formed by common carotid, inferior thyroid artery, and recurrent nerve), and the ligament of Berry.

image.brief: Operative field through a Kocher collar neck incision showing the thyroid lobe retracted medially, middle thyroid vein divided, and recurrent laryngeal nerve exposed in the groove.

items.summary: En bloc resection of entire breast with nipple-areola complex and Level I/II axillary lymph nodes while preserving pectoralis major and minor muscles.

blocks.title: Indications and incision
bullets: Standard curative operation for operable breast carcinoma where breast-conserving therapy is contraindicated or declined.
Contraindications to breast conservation: multicentric disease, diffuse microcalcifications, large tumour-to-breast ratio, prior radiation.
Patient positioned supine with ipsilateral arm abducted to 90 degrees on an arm board.
Stewart transverse elliptical incision or Orr oblique incision enclosing the tumour, previous biopsy scar, and nipple-areola complex with 1 cm skin margin.

blocks.title: Key operative steps in outline
bullets: Thin skin flaps raised in the subcutaneous plane: superior flap up to clavicle; inferior flap down to rectus abdominis sheath.
Medial limit reaches lateral border of sternum; lateral limit reaches anterior border of latissimus dorsi muscle.
Breast tissue dissected sharply off the pectoralis major muscle along with the pectoral fascia from medial to lateral.
Axillary dissection: axillary vein identified and unroofed; Level I and Level II lymph nodes dissected en bloc.
Long thoracic nerve (of Bell) identified and preserved along the medial axillary wall lying on serratus anterior.
Thoracodorsal neurovascular bundle identified and preserved along the lateral axillary wall entering latissimus dorsi.
Two closed-suction drains placed (one in axilla, one under pectoral flaps); skin flaps approximated in two layers.

blocks.title: Complications and nerve injuries
bullets: Injury to long thoracic nerve produces serratus anterior paralysis resulting in classic 'winged scapula' (scapula alata).
Injury to thoracodorsal nerve paralyzes latissimus dorsi, impairing adduction, internal rotation, and pulling down of the shoulder.
Intercostobrachial nerve division produces numbness over the inner aspect of the upper arm and axilla.
Late postoperative complications: seroma beneath flaps, flap necrosis, and chronic secondary upper limb lymphedema.

viva.q: What is the anatomical difference between Halsted radical mastectomy and Patey modified radical mastectomy?
viva.a: Halsted resects pectoralis major and minor muscles plus Level I-III nodes; Patey preserves pectoralis major (often resecting minor) with Level I-II nodes, yielding equal survival.

viva.q: What clinical deformity results from iatrogenic injury to the long thoracic nerve of Bell?
viva.a: Winging of the scapula (scapula alata) due to paralysis of the serratus anterior muscle, prominent when the patient pushes forward against a wall.

viva.q: Which three nerves are encountered in the axilla during axillary lymph node dissection?
viva.a: The long thoracic nerve of Bell (supplies serratus anterior), thoracodorsal nerve (supplies latissimus dorsi), and intercostobrachial nerve (sensory to inner arm).

image.brief: Operative field illustration of a modified radical mastectomy showing the chest wall with pectoralis major exposed, axillary vein unroofed, and long thoracic nerve preserved on serratus anterior.

items.summary: Open surgical excision of prolapsed third and fourth-degree internal haemorrhoids at 3, 7, and 11 o'clock positions leaving mucosal skin bridges.

blocks.title: Indications and positioning
bullets: Indicated for Grade III and Grade IV internal haemorrhoids, strangulated piles, or mixed internal-external haemorrhoidal complexes.
Position: lithotomy position with buttocks positioned slightly over the edge of the operating table.
Anaesthesia: spinal (saddle block), caudal epidural, or local perineal infiltration block.
Perianal skin prepared with antiseptic solution; Parks self-retaining bivalve anal retractor or Eisenhammer retractor inserted.

blocks.title: Key operative steps in outline
bullets: Inspect the anal canal to confirm the three primary piles at left lateral (3 o'clock), right anterior (11 o'clock), and right posterior (7 o'clock).
Apply artery forceps to the perianal skin tag and another forceps to the mucosal apex of the internal haemorrhoid for traction.
V-shaped incision made in the perianal skin around the external component extending upwards into the anal canal.
Haemorrhoidal plexus dissected off the underlying circular fibres of the internal anal sphincter using scissors or diathermy.
Dissection continued to the pedicle above the anorectal ring; pedicle transfixed and ligated securely with 2-0 chromic catgut or Vicryl.
Excess haemorrhoidal tissue excised 5 mm distal to the ligature.
Crucial rule: leave generous mucosal and skin bridges between the excision wounds to prevent postoperative anal canal stenosis.
Wounds are left open to heal by secondary intention (open technique); anal pack or hemostatic dressing inserted.

blocks.title: Complications and postoperative care
bullets: Primary, reactionary, or secondary haemorrhage (secondary bleeding occurs on days 7 to 10 from ligature sloughing).
Urinary retention is common (20% to 30%) due to reflex perineal pelvic floor muscle spasm.
Severe anal stenosis or stricture if skin bridges are inadvertently sacrificed or excised.
Postoperative care: warm sitz baths, high-roughage diet, stool softeners, and adequate multimodal analgesia.

viva.q: Why are primary internal haemorrhoids located at the 3, 7, and 11 o'clock positions?
viva.a: They correspond to the terminal branches of the superior rectal artery, which divides into right and left branches; the right divides into anterior (11) and posterior (7) branches.

viva.q: Why is it absolutely vital to leave wide skin and mucosal bridges during Milligan-Morgan haemorrhoidectomy?
viva.a: To ensure rapid epithelialisation from the edges and prevent circumferential scarring, cicatrisation, and severe postoperative anal stricture.

viva.q: How does the Ferguson haemorrhoidectomy differ from the Milligan-Morgan procedure?
viva.a: Ferguson is a closed haemorrhoidectomy where mucosal and skin edges are sutured closed; Milligan-Morgan is an open procedure left to heal by secondary intention.

image.brief: Perianal operative view in lithotomy position showing Parks retractor in place with clover-leaf excision of piles at 3, 7, and 11 o'clock, with wide mucosal bridges between wounds.

items.summary: Surgical repair of primary vaginal hydrocele by opening the tunica vaginalis sac, aspirating fluid, and everting the sac behind the testis.

blocks.title: Indications and anaesthesia
bullets: Indicated for primary vaginal hydrocele with a moderate to large, thickened tunica vaginalis sac.
Contraindicated in secondary hydrocele due to testicular tumour; always perform scrotal ultrasound before surgery to exclude underlying malignancy.
Performed under local scrotal infiltration, spinal anaesthesia, or general anaesthesia.
Incision: transverse or longitudinal scrotal incision through skin and dartos muscle in an avascular scrotal crease.

blocks.title: Key operative steps in outline
bullets: Incision deepened through external spermatic fascia, cremasteric muscle, and internal spermatic fascia to reach parietal tunica vaginalis.
Tense hydrocele sac mobilised and delivered through the scrotal wound by gentle gauze dissection.
Small incision made in the sac and clear amber hydrocele fluid aspirated using a wide cannula or suction.
Sac opened along its entire length from upper to lower pole, taking care not to injure the testis, epididymis, or vas deferens.
Redundant portions of the thickened sac excised, leaving adequate borders for tension-free eversion.
Cut edges of the tunica vaginalis are everted (turned inside out) behind the testis and epididymis.
Edges sutured together behind the spermatic cord and epididymis using a continuous absorbable suture (Jaboulay eversion).
Testis returned to the hemiscrotum in correct orientation without twisting the spermatic cord; dartos and skin closed in layers.

blocks.title: Complications and postoperative care
bullets: Scrotal haematoma is the commonest and most troublesome complication; meticulous hemostasis of sac edges is mandatory.
Scrotal oedema, wound infection, and injury to the testicular vessels or vas deferens.
Postoperative scrotal support (suspensory bandage or tight brief) is worn for two weeks to minimize dependent oedema.

viva.q: What is the anatomical objective of the Jaboulay procedure?
viva.a: To evert the visceral mesothelial lining of the tunica vaginalis outward so fluid is absorbed by scrotal lymphatics rather than trapped in a closed sac.

viva.q: Why must meticulous hemostasis be achieved before closing a scrotal incision?
viva.a: The lax, corrugated dartos and subcutaneous scrotal tissues provide little natural tissue resistance, predisposing to massive expansile scrotal haematoma formation.

viva.q: How does the Jaboulay procedure differ from Lord plication for hydrocele?
viva.a: Jaboulay mobilises and everts the sac behind the testis with edge suturing; Lord plication does not mobilise the sac, but gathers and plicates it in situ.

image.brief: Operative view showing the tunica vaginalis sac split open, testis delivered, and the edges of the sac everted and sutured together behind the epididymis with continuous absorbable suture.

title.en: Lord plication procedure for primary hydrocele

items.summary: Surgical repair of a thin-walled primary vaginal hydrocele by radially plicating the opened sac edges without extensive tissue mobilisation.

blocks.title: Indications and surgical concept
bullets: Indicated for small to moderate primary vaginal hydroceles with a thin, pliable, non-fibrotic tunica vaginalis sac.
Devised by Peter Lord in 1964 to eliminate extensive scrotal dissection and minimize the incidence of postoperative scrotal haematoma.
Contraindicated when the sac wall is thick, calcified, fibrotic, or multilocular, where Jaboulay or excision is required.
Incision: small 3 to 4 cm transverse scrotal incision made directly over the anterior aspect of the hydrocele.

blocks.title: Key operative steps in outline
bullets: Scrotal skin, dartos, and fascial coverings incised directly down to the parietal tunica vaginalis without dissecting planes.
Small stab incision made into the sac, hydrocele fluid evacuated completely by suction, and sac opened widely longitudinally.
Testis and epididymis extruded through the small incision, causing the tunica vaginalis to turn inside out naturally.
Eight to twelve interrupted or continuous radial gathering sutures (2-0 chromic catgut or Vicryl) placed around the perimeter of the sac.
Each stitch catches the cut edge of the sac, traverses the plicated tunic, and catches the junction near the testis-epididymal groove.
Sutures tied sequentially, reefing and gathering the entire sac into a compact, corrugated collar around the testicular rete.
Testis replaced into the scrotal pouch; dartos and skin closed in layers with absorbable sutures.

blocks.title: Complications and advantages
bullets: Major advantage: virtually zero risk of postoperative haematoma because tissue planes in the scrotum are never opened or stripped.
Rapid operative time (typically 10 to 15 minutes) and can be performed as an outpatient daycare procedure under local anaesthesia.
Complications: stitch granuloma, transient scrotal swelling, and recurrence if sutures tear out of an inappropriately thickened sac.

viva.q: What is the cardinal surgical advantage of Lord plication over traditional Jaboulay eversion?
viva.a: Lord plication leaves the outer fascial planes undisturbed without mobilising the sac from the scrotum, drastically reducing the risk of postoperative haematoma.

viva.q: When is Lord plication contraindicated in hydrocele surgery?
viva.a: In long-standing hydroceles with thickened, fibrotic, rigid, or calcified sacs, which cannot be gathered and plicated effectively.

viva.q: How are the plication sutures placed during the Lord procedure?
viva.a: Radially oriented gathering sutures are placed through the full thickness of the folded sac from the outer cut edge to its reflection near the epididymis.

image.brief: Operative diagram showing the testis extruded through a small scrotal incision with radial gathering sutures placed around the redundant tunica vaginalis to plicate it into a collar.

items.summary: Surgical excision of the redundant prepuce and inner mucosal collar with restoration of the coronal sulcus using absorbable sutures.

blocks.title: Indications and techniques
bullets: Indicated for pathological phimosis, recurrent balanoposthitis, paraphimosis, balanitis xerotica obliterans (BXO), and religious requirements.
Absolute contraindications: hypospadias and chordee, where prepuce is required for future reconstructive urethroplasty.
Anaesthesia: dorsal penile nerve block combined with ring block at the penile base using 1% plain lignocaine (NEVER use adrenaline).
Techniques: dorsal slit method, sleeve resection method, or clamp techniques (Gomco clamp, Plastibell in neonates).

blocks.title: Key operative steps in outline (Sleeve technique)
bullets: Prepuce retracted, smegma cleaned, and physiological adhesions between inner prepuce and glans divided bluntly with gauze.
Two circular circumferential skin incisions marked: outer incision at level of coronal sulcus; inner incision 5 mm proximal to corona.
Dorsal slit created between two straight artery forceps applied to the prepuce at 11 and 1 o'clock positions.
Sleeve of preputial skin between inner and outer incised lines excised sharply with scissors.
Frenular artery isolated at 6 o'clock and securely ligated with a fine 3-0 or 4-0 absorbable mattress suture (frenular stitch).
Meticulous bipolar hemostasis achieved; adrenaline must never be used due to terminal end-artery vasospasm and glans gangrene.
Skin edges approximated to the inner mucosal collar using interrupted 4-0 chromic catgut or rapid Vicryl sutures.
Paraffin gauze or light non-adherent dressing applied around the coronal suture line.

blocks.title: Complications and surgical warnings
bullets: Reactionary haemorrhage from the frenular artery is the commonest emergency complication.
Excessive skin removal causing penile denudation or insufficient skin removal causing persistent redundancy.
Meatal stenosis (especially after BXO or neonatal circumcision), wound infection, and accidental glans injury.

viva.q: Why is adrenaline strictly contraindicated in local anaesthetic solutions used for circumcision?
viva.a: The penile blood supply consists of terminal end-arteries; adrenaline causes intense, prolonged vasospasm leading to ischaemic necrosis and gangrene of the glans penis.

viva.q: Why is hypospadias an absolute contraindication to circumcision?
viva.a: Because the hooded dorsal prepuce provides essential, vascularised skin tissue needed for reconstructive urethroplasty to correct the ventral meatal defect.

viva.q: What is paraphimosis and how is it managed immediately?
viva.a: A retracted tight prepuce trapped behind the corona causing glans oedema; managed by manual compression to reduce swelling followed by reduction, or emergency dorsal slit.

image.brief: Operative drawing showing circumcision sleeve resection with dorsal slit made, redundant preputial sleeve excised, and interrupted absorbable sutures placed around the corona.

title.en: Incision and drainage of an abscess (Hilton method)

items.summary: Surgical drainage of pyogenic soft tissue abscess under local or general anaesthesia along skin Langer lines following Hilton method.

blocks.title: Indications and principles
bullets: Indicated for any collection of pus in soft tissues demonstrating fluctuance (e.g. subcutaneous, breast, perianal, or ischiorectal abscess).
Cardinal surgical principle: 'Ubi pus, ibi evacua' (where there is pus, evacuate it); antibiotics cannot penetrate an avascular abscess cavity.
Anaesthesia: general anaesthesia or field/regional block; do not inject local anaesthetic directly into the infected acidic cavity.
Incision placed along relaxed skin tension lines (Langer lines) over the site of maximum fluctuance and dependent drainage.

blocks.title: Key operative steps in outline (Hilton method)
bullets: Skin incised sharply through dermis only along Langer lines over the point of maximum fluctuance.
Closed sinus forceps or blunt hemostat introduced into the abscess cavity through the incision.
Forceps blades opened widely within the cavity and withdrawn in the open position to enlarge the track without cutting vessels.
Pus evacuated completely; swab collected immediately and sent for Gram stain, aerobic, and anaerobic microbiological culture.
Gloved index finger introduced into the cavity to explore and gently break down all internal loculi and septations.
Cavity irrigated copiously with warm normal saline until effluent is clear of necrotic debris.
Corrugated rubber drain, Yeates drain, or loose sterile ribbon gauze pack placed to maintain open dependent drainage and prevent premature skin closure.

blocks.title: Complications and special sites
bullets: Perianal abscess: drainage must be placed close to the anal verge to keep any secondary fistula-in-ano tract as short as possible.
Breast abscess: radial incision used to avoid transecting lactiferous ducts; submammary incision (Gaillard-Thomas) for deep abscesses.
Complications: incomplete drainage with recurrent abscess, injury to adjacent neurovascular structures, and chronic sinus or fistula.

viva.q: What is the Hilton method of draining deep abscesses and why is it used?
viva.a: Incising skin only, then introducing closed sinus forceps and opening them widely to breach the abscess; it prevents iatrogenic injury to neighbouring vital nerves and vessels.

viva.q: Why does local anaesthetic infiltration fail when injected directly into an acute abscess?
viva.a: The low pH of purulent tissue ionises the local anaesthetic, preventing the unionised base form from traversing nerve sheaths to block sodium channels.

viva.q: Why must internal loculi be systematically broken down with a finger during abscess drainage?
viva.a: Pyogenic abscesses are frequently multiloculated; failure to break down all fibrous septa leaves trapped pockets of pus, causing rapid recurrence.

image.brief: Surgical illustration showing an incision over a fluctuant abscess along Langer lines with sinus forceps inserted and opened widely to evacuate pus without vessel injury.

title.en: Surgical wound debridement and wound toilet

items.summary: Systematic surgical excision of devitalised, contaminated skin, fat, fascia, and non-contractile muscle from traumatic open wounds.

blocks.title: Principles and indications
bullets: Mandatory procedure for open traumatic wounds, compound fractures, crush injuries, contaminated lacerations, and necrotising fasciitis.
Objective: convert a contaminated, ragged traumatic wound with dead tissue into a clean, vascularised surgical wound.
Timing: perform as early as possible within the 6-hour golden period before bacterial colonisation progresses to invasive tissue infection.
Copious low-pressure irrigation using normal saline (typically 6 to 9 litres for severe open fractures) to wash out debris.

blocks.title: Key operative steps in outline
bullets: Wound washed, surrounding skin shaved, painted with antiseptic, and draped; foreign material, dirt, and gravel mechanically removed.
Skin edges: excise a minimal margin (1 to 2 mm) of clearly devitalised, ragged, non-bleeding epidermal edge.
Subcutaneous fat: generous excision of all bruised, crushed, avascular, or contaminated fat, which has poor resistance to infection.
Deep fascia: opened widely along the long axis of the limb to relieve compartment pressure and expose all underlying muscles.
Muscle debridement: assess viability using the classic 'Four Cs' and excise all non-viable muscle until healthy tissue is reached.
Bone fragments: remove small, loose, unattached bone fragments devoid of periosteal blood supply; preserve large articular fragments.
Leave traumatic wound open for secondary inspection (second-look debridement at 48 hours) or delayed primary closure.

blocks.title: The Four Cs of muscle viability and complications
bullets: Four Cs of muscle viability: Colour (red vs dark purple/brown), Consistency (firm/resilient vs mushy/friable).
Contractility (contracts when pinched with forceps or stimulated), and Capillary bleeding (oozes bright red blood when cut).
Complications: missed deep contamination leading to gas gangrene (Clostridium perfringens), tetanus, or chronic osteomyelitis.

viva.q: What are the classic 'Four Cs' used intraoperatively to judge muscle viability during debridement?
viva.a: Colour (normal reddish-pink), Consistency (firm and elastic), Contractility (brisk twitch when pinched with forceps), and Capillary bleeding (fresh punctate bleeding when incised).

viva.q: Why should high-energy traumatic open wounds generally not be closed primarily after initial debridement?
viva.a: Because residual borderline tissue may necrose over the next 48 hours, creating an anaerobic environment beneath closed skin that fosters fatal clostridial gas gangrene.

viva.q: What is delayed primary closure (DPC)?
viva.a: Wound closure performed between the 3rd and 5th postoperative day after initial debridement, once the wound is inspected and confirmed clean and free of infection.

image.brief: Operative view of a traumatic lower limb wound showing wide fasciotomy, wound irrigation with saline, and forceps testing muscle contractility and bleeding capacity.

items.summary: Harvesting an epidermal and partial dermal skin graft using a Humby knife or dermatome and securing it over a vascularised recipient wound bed.

blocks.title: Indications and graft thickness
bullets: Indicated for covering extensive cutaneous defects: major burns, large traumatic skin loss, fasciotomy wounds, and post-excision defects.
Split-thickness skin graft (STSG) comprises the entire epidermis and a variable portion of the underlying dermis.
Subtypes: thin Thiersch graft, intermediate split graft, and thick split-thickness graft.
Common donor sites: anterolateral aspect of the thigh, buttocks, medial arm, or abdominal wall.

blocks.title: Key operative steps in outline
bullets: Recipient bed prepared: must consist of healthy, flat, vascular, red granulation tissue free of beta-haemolytic streptococci and slough.
Donor thigh lubricated with sterile liquid paraffin; assistant holds wooden board to flatten skin ahead of the blade.
Humby knife (or electric dermatome) held at a 30-degree angle; graft harvested with a steady, smooth sawing motion.
Graft meshed (1:1.5 or 1:3 ratio) using a skin graft mesher to expand surface area and permit fluid drainage.
Graft laid on the recipient bed dermal-side down, smoothed out to eliminate air pockets, and anchored with staples or 4-0 sutures.
Tie-over bolster dressing (stent dressing) applied using paraffin gauze and saline-soaked cotton balls secured with long suture ends.
Donor site dressed with hemostatic calcium alginate or paraffin gauze and left undisturbed for 10 to 14 days to re-epithelialise.

blocks.title: Graft take phases and causes of failure
bullets: Three phases of graft take: Plasmatic imbibition (first 24 to 48 hours, absorbs nutrients by capillary action), Inosculation (48 to 72 hours, vascular anastomoses), and Revascularisation.
Commonest cause of graft failure is haematoma or seroma elevating the graft away from its bed, followed by shearing motion and infection.
Heavy bacterial bioburden or Streptococcus pyogenes infection rapidly destroys the graft.

viva.q: What are the three chronological phases of skin graft survival ('take')?
viva.a: Plasmatic imbibition (first 24-48 hours, passive nutrient absorption), inosculation (days 2-3, microvascular alignment and connection), and neovascularisation (ingrowth of donor and recipient capillaries).

viva.q: What are the commonest causes of split-thickness skin graft failure?
viva.a: Haematoma or seroma collection under the graft (most common), mechanical shearing movement displacing capillary connections, and infection (especially Streptococcus pyogenes).

viva.q: How does the donor site heal following harvest of a split-thickness skin graft?
viva.a: By spontaneous re-epithelialisation originating from residual epidermal appendages preserved in the deep reticular dermis (hair follicles, sebaceous glands, and sweat ducts).

image.brief: Surgical field view showing a meshed split-thickness skin graft placed over a clean granulated wound bed on the lower leg with long tie-over bolster sutures positioned.

items.summary: Harvesting a cutaneous graft comprising epidermis and the entire dermis, defatting, and insetting into small facial or flexural defects.

blocks.title: Indications and characteristics
bullets: Indicated for small, cosmetically sensitive defects on the face (eyelids, nasal tip, cheeks) and flexion creases of the hands and fingers.
Contains the entire epidermis and full thickness of dermis including dermal skin appendages (sweat and sebaceous glands).
Advantages: superior colour and texture match, minimal secondary contraction (preserves elasticity), and durable skin coverage.
Common donor sites: postauricular sulcus, upper eyelid, supraclavicular fossa, and groin crease.

blocks.title: Key operative steps in outline
bullets: Exact template of the recipient defect created using a sterile foil or gauze pattern.
Template traced onto the donor site along Langer relaxed skin tension lines to allow primary donor closure.
Incision made through the skin down to the junction of the dermis and subcutaneous fat.
Graft excised sharply; crucial step: meticulous defatting of the graft undersurface using curved iris scissors until glistening white dermis is exposed.
Subcutaneous fat is an avascular barrier that blocks plasmatic imbibition and prevents revascularisation.
Graft inset into the recipient defect, sutured with interrupted 5-0 or 6-0 monofilament sutures, leaving long suture ends.
Tie-over bolster dressing tied securely over paraffin gauze to exert uniform compression and prevent seroma accumulation.
Donor site closed primarily in layers with aesthetic skin closure.

blocks.title: Differences from split-thickness grafts
bullets: Full-thickness graft requires a more vascular recipient bed because its thicker dermis demands higher metabolic support during take.
Primary contracture (immediate shrinkage upon harvesting) is high due to intact dermal elastin fibres.
Secondary contracture (scar shrinkage during healing) is minimal compared to STSG, preventing flexural contractures.
Donor site cannot re-epithelialise spontaneously and must be closed primarily with sutures.

viva.q: Why is meticulous defatting of a full-thickness Wolfe graft mandatory before insetting?
viva.a: Subcutaneous fat is an avascular, hydrophobic insulator that prevents host plasmatic fluid and capillary sprouts from penetrating the dermis, causing complete graft necrosis.

viva.q: Why does a full-thickness graft undergo less secondary contraction than a split-thickness graft?
viva.a: Because it contains the complete dermis, which physically resists myofibroblast-mediated wound contraction and scar retraction during long-term healing.

viva.q: What are the preferred donor sites for harvesting a full-thickness skin graft for facial defects?
viva.a: Postauricular skin, upper eyelid, and supraclavicular fossa; they offer excellent thinness, dermal compliance, and high colour and texture match with facial skin.

image.brief: Surgical photograph showing an excised circular full-thickness skin graft being meticulously defatted with fine curved scissors until glistening white reticular dermis is exposed.

items.summary: Surgical creation of an artificial airway opening into the anterior cervical trachea between the 2nd and 3rd rings for acute obstruction.

blocks.title: Indications and positioning
bullets: Indicated for acute upper airway obstruction (laryngeal trauma, foreign body, Ludwig angina, malignancy), prolonged mechanical ventilation, and bronchial hygiene.
Patient positioned supine with a shoulder roll to extend the neck, head in the midline (avoid over-extension in unstable cervical spine trauma).
Anaesthesia: local infiltration with 1% or 2% lignocaine with adrenaline in the midline, or general anaesthesia if endotracheal tube is already in situ.
Incision: transverse skin crease incision 2 cm below cricoid cartilage, or vertical midline incision from cricoid to suprasternal notch.

blocks.title: Key operative steps in outline
bullets: Skin and platysma incised; investing layer of deep cervical fascia opened vertically in the true midline between anterior jugular veins.
Strap muscles (sternohyoid and sternothyroid) retracted laterally using Langenbeck retractors.
Thyroid isthmus identified crossing the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th tracheal rings; isthmus retracted superiorly or divided between transfixion ligatures.
Pretracheal fascia cleared to expose the glistening anterior surface of the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th tracheal rings.
Cricoid hook placed under the cricoid cartilage to pull the trachea upward and steady it in the midline.
Tracheal window created: transverse incision or inverted U-shaped flap (Bjork flap) between the 2nd and 3rd tracheal rings.
Never incise the 1st tracheal ring to prevent secondary subglottic stenosis.
Cuffed tracheostomy tube of appropriate size inserted under direct vision; cuff inflated, tube tied securely around the neck with cotton tapes.
Verify bilateral air entry by chest auscultation and end-tidal carbon dioxide monitoring.

blocks.title: Complications and emergency precautions
bullets: Immediate: haemorrhage (inferior thyroid veins, thyroid isthmus), pneumothorax, air embolism, and surgical emphysema.
Late: tracheo-innominate artery fistula (massive sentinel bleeding), tracheal stenosis, and tracheo-oesophageal fistula.
Accidental decannulation within the first 48 hours is a life-threatening crisis because the tract has not matured; reinsert under vision.

viva.q: Why must the first tracheal ring never be incised during a tracheostomy?
viva.a: Incising the first ring or cricoid cartilage induces chondritis and severe cicatricial subglottic stenosis, which is extremely difficult to reconstruct surgically.

viva.q: What is a Bjork flap in tracheostomy?
viva.a: An inverted U-shaped flap created in the anterior wall of the 2nd and 3rd tracheal rings, sutured to the inferior skin edge to facilitate safe tube changes.

viva.q: What is the most catastrophic delayed vascular complication of a low tracheostomy?
viva.a: Tracheo-innominate artery fistula, caused by high cuff pressure or low tube tip eroding the brachiocephalic (innominate) artery, causing torrential bleeding.

image.brief: Operative view through a cervical neck incision showing strap muscles retracted, thyroid isthmus divided, and cricoid hook elevating the trachea with a tracheostomy tube being introduced.

items.summary: Placement of a chest drain into the pleural cavity within the safe triangle, connected to an underwater seal drainage system.

blocks.title: Indications and the safe triangle
bullets: Indicated for pneumothorax, tension pneumothorax (following needle decompression), haemothorax, empyema thoracis, and malignant effusion.
The 'safe triangle' of the British Thoracic Society minimizes damage to internal thoracic, long thoracic, and lateral thoracic vessels.
Boundaries of the safe triangle: anterior border of latissimus dorsi posteriorly, lateral border of pectoralis major anteriorly, and 5th intercostal space inferiorly.
Patient positioned semi-recumbent at 45 degrees with ipsilateral arm abducted and hand placed behind the patient's head.

blocks.title: Key operative steps in outline
bullets: Skin and subcutaneous tissues infiltrated with 1% or 2% lignocaine down to the periosteum of the rib and parietal pleura.
Transverse 2 to 3 cm skin incision placed in the 5th intercostal space along the anterior axillary line.
Incision placed over the rib immediately below the target intercostal space to create an oblique subcutaneous tunnel.
Blunt dissection performed with curved Kelly or Spencer Wells forceps over the superior border of the 6th rib (avoiding neurovascular bundle under the 5th rib).
Parietal pleura breached with forceps tip; gloved index finger introduced into the pleural space to verify position and sweep adhesions.
Large-bore chest tube (28 to 32 Fr for haemothorax; 20 to 24 Fr for pneumothorax) clamped and guided into the apical or basal pleural space.
All side-eye holes of the tube must lie entirely inside the pleural space.
Tube connected immediately to an underwater seal drainage bottle; confirm respiratory swinging (tidalling) in the water column.
Tube secured with heavy non-absorbable suture (e.g. 1-0 silk) and wrapped with petroleum gauze dressing.

blocks.title: Complications and removal criteria
bullets: Injury to intercostal neurovascular bundle by dissecting along the inferior rib border causes severe bleeding.
Trocar insertion risks catastrophic lung laceration, cardiac puncture, or intra-abdominal liver/splenic perforation; NEVER use sharp trocars blindly.
Removal criteria: lung fully expanded on chest radiograph, no air leak on coughing, and drainage less than 50 to 100 ml per 24 hours.

viva.q: What are the anatomical boundaries of the 'safe triangle' for chest drain insertion?
viva.a: Anteriorly by the lateral border of pectoralis major, posteriorly by the anterior border of latissimus dorsi, and inferiorly by the horizontal line of the 5th intercostal space.

viva.q: Why must the dissecting instrument always pass over the upper border of the rib rather than the lower border?
viva.a: The intercostal vein, artery, and nerve (VAN from above downward) run sheltered in the subcostal groove along the lower border of each rib.

viva.q: What is 'respiratory swinging' (tidalling) in an underwater seal drainage system?
viva.a: The fluid meniscus inside the underwater tube rises during inspiration (negative intrapleural pressure) and falls during expiration, confirming the tube is patent and within the pleural space.

image.brief: Clinical photograph showing an intercostal chest tube inserted in the 5th space within the safe triangle, secured with mattress suture and connected to an underwater seal glass chamber.

items.summary: Radical excision of the testis and spermatic cord up to the internal inguinal ring through a groin incision for suspected testicular malignancy.

blocks.title: Indications and oncological principle
bullets: Gold standard diagnostic and therapeutic operation for any suspected malignant testicular tumour (seminoma or non-seminoma).
Cardinal oncological rule: NEVER perform scrotal incision or percutaneous needle biopsy for a testicular mass.
Trans-scrotal entry breaches anatomical fascial barriers and contaminates superficial inguinal lymphatic drainage pathways.
Incision: standard inguinal incision placed 2 cm above and parallel to the medial two-thirds of the inguinal ligament.

blocks.title: Key operative steps in outline
bullets: External oblique aponeurosis opened in the line of its fibres from the superficial ring to above the deep internal ring.
Spermatic cord mobilised immediately at the deep inguinal ring and atraumatically soft-clamped to prevent intraoperative haematogenous embolisation.
Spermatic cord dissected free from the floor of the canal down towards the scrotal neck.
Gloved hand exerts upward pressure from the scrotum to deliver the intact testis, surrounded by its tunics, into the groin wound.
Testis inspected and palpated; if malignancy is confirmed, the cord is doubly ligated at the internal ring and transected.
Vas deferens and testicular vascular pedicle ligated separately with non-absorbable sutures (e.g. 1-0 silk) to prevent slippage.
Hemostasis confirmed; external oblique closed; inguinal canal reconstructed; scrotal skin left undisturbed.

blocks.title: Complications and staging
bullets: Retroperitoneal haematoma from slipped high cord ligature.
Surgical site haematoma or seroma in the scrotum or inguinal canal.
Resected specimen sent intact for histopathology, including margins of the spermatic cord.
Postoperative serum tumour markers (AFP, beta-hCG, LDH) monitored to assess clearance according to half-lives.

viva.q: Why is early vascular clamping of the spermatic cord performed at the internal ring during orchidectomy?
viva.a: To occlude testicular venous and lymphatic drainage prior to mobilising and manipulating the tumour-bearing testis, preventing intraoperative haematogenous tumor dissemination.

viva.q: What is the biological half-life of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and beta-hCG?
viva.a: AFP half-life is 5 to 7 days; beta-hCG half-life is 24 to 36 hours; persistence beyond expected clearance indicates residual metastatic disease.

viva.q: What are the indications for partial orchidectomy (testis-sparing surgery)?
viva.a: Synchronous bilateral testicular tumours, tumour in a solitary functioning testis, or small benign stromal lesions under 2 cm with normal marker levels.

image.brief: Operative field through an inguinal incision showing the spermatic cord clamped with a soft vascular bulldog clamp at the deep ring and the intact testis delivered into the wound.

items.summary: Flush ligation of the great saphenous vein at its confluence with the common femoral vein, with division of all tributary branches.

blocks.title: Indications and landmarks
bullets: Indicated for primary varicose veins secondary to saphenofemoral junction (SFJ) valve incompetence.
Landmark: saphenofemoral junction lies 4 cm below and 4 cm lateral to the pubic tubercle.
Femoral artery pulsation palpated lateral to the junction as an essential anatomical guide.
Incision: transverse groin crease incision placed 1 cm above and parallel to the groin crease, centered over the saphenous opening.

blocks.title: Key operative steps in outline
bullets: Incision deepened through superficial Camper fascia and membranous Scarpa fascia to expose the fossa ovalis.
Great saphenous vein identified emerging through the cribriform fascia to join the common femoral vein.
All six constant SFJ tributaries dissected, ligated, and divided: superficial circumflex iliac, superficial epigastric, external pudendal, and medial or lateral accessory saphenous veins.
Failure to divide even one tributary leads to postoperative recurrent varicose veins through collateral channels.
Great saphenous vein dissected right up to its flush anatomical confluence with the medial aspect of the common femoral vein.
Saphenofemoral junction flush-ligated with non-absorbable suture (1-0 silk) and transfixed without narrowing the lumen of the femoral vein.
Great saphenous trunk can then be stripped down to knee level using a Myers flexible vein stripper.
Wound closed in layers with absorbable subcutaneous sutures.

blocks.title: Complications and surgical traps
bullets: Iatrogenic ligation or injury of the common femoral vein: devastating error mistaking femoral vein for saphenous vein.
Injury to femoral artery (lying lateral) or femoral nerve.
Lymph fistula, lymphatic leak, or groin wound infection resulting from transection of inguinal lymph nodes and channels.
Deep venous thrombosis (DVT) from thermal injury, intimal trauma, or constriction of the common femoral vein.

viva.q: Why must the great saphenous vein be ligated strictly flush with the common femoral vein?
viva.a: Leaving a residual blind saphenous stump allows tributary veins to dilate over time, forming a venous reservoir that causes recurrent varicose veins.

viva.q: Name the six tributaries that enter the great saphenous vein near the saphenofemoral junction.
viva.a: Superficial epigastric, superficial circumflex iliac, superficial external pudendal, deep external pudendal, anterolateral accessory saphenous, and posteromedial accessory saphenous veins.

viva.q: How do you distinguish the great saphenous vein from the common femoral vein intraoperatively?
viva.a: The saphenous vein receives superficial tributaries and enters the anterior-medial aspect of the larger femoral vein, which has no anterior tributaries and continues proximally.

image.brief: Surgical field view through a right groin crease incision showing the saphenofemoral junction with all tributary veins ligated and a flush transfixion suture placed on the saphenous trunk.

items.summary: Surgical creation of a temporary defunctioning dual-lumen stoma from the distal ileum through the right rectus muscle with a Brooke everted spout.

blocks.title: Indications and stoma site marking
bullets: Indicated to protect low pelvic colorectal or coloanal anastomoses (e.g. low anterior resection, ileal pouch-anal anastomosis).
Reduces the clinical consequences and sepsis of anastomotic leak, though it does not prevent leak occurrence.
Preoperative stoma siting: marked within the rectus abdominis muscle, away from scars, skin folds, umbilicus, and waist belt line.
Sited at the summit of the infra-umbilical abdominal fat roll in standing, sitting, and supine positions.

blocks.title: Key operative steps in outline
bullets: Circular skin disc (approximately 2.5 cm diameter) excised at the pre-marked right iliac fossa site.
Subcutaneous fat excised; anterior rectus sheath incised vertically; rectus abdominis muscle split bluntly in the line of fibres.
Posterior rectus sheath and peritoneum opened to permit two fingers to pass easily through the abdominal wall trephine.
Loop of distal ileum selected approximately 15 to 20 cm proximal to the ileocaecal valve, ensuring adequate mesenteric mobility.
Orientation verified: proximal functional limb oriented inferiorly; distal non-functional limb oriented superiorly.
Plastic stoma rod or bridge passed through an avascular window in the mesentery to support the exteriorised loop on the skin.
Transverse enterotomy created in the distal non-functional aspect of the loop across two-thirds of its circumference.
Brooke eversion performed on the proximal limb using 3-0 absorbable sutures, fashioning a 2 to 3 cm protruding spout.
Protruding spout directs corrosive, enzyme-rich liquid ileal effluent directly into the appliance bag without skin contact.

blocks.title: Complications and management
bullets: Peristomal skin excoriation caused by corrosive proteolytic digestive enzymes in high-output ileal discharge.
High-output stoma (>1500 ml/day) causing profound dehydration, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, and prerenal acute kidney injury.
Other complications: stoma retraction, prolapse, ischemia/necrosis of the exteriorized loop, and parastomal hernia.

viva.q: Why is a loop ileostomy constructed with an everted protruding spout (Brooke eversion)?
viva.a: To project corrosive liquid ileal chyme rich in proteolytic enzymes directly into the stoma bag, preventing direct chemical contact and excoriation of peristomal skin.

viva.q: Why is the stoma trephine always passed through the rectus abdominis muscle belly?
viva.a: The surrounding muscular corset provides dynamic support and stabilizes the stoma, significantly reducing the long-term risk of parastomal herniation.

viva.q: What defines a high-output stoma and what is the initial medical management?
viva.a: Effluent exceeding 1500 to 2000 ml per 24 hours; managed by fluid/electrolyte replacement, antimotility agents (loperamide), and oral rehydration solution (ORS).

image.brief: Operative photograph of a matured loop ileostomy in the right iliac fossa supported on a plastic stoma rod, displaying a 2.5 cm everted pink mucosal spout and proximal active lumen.

items.summary: Surgical creation of a defunctioning loop stoma using the mobile sigmoid colon supported over an external stoma bridge in the left lower quadrant.

blocks.title: Indications and anatomical position
bullets: Indicated for decompression of distal acute mechanical colonic obstruction (rectal cancer, diverticular stricture), rectal injury, or complex perineal trauma.
Preoperative siting: marked within the left rectus abdominis muscle in the left lower quadrant along the spinoumbilical line.
Requires a mobile, redundant sigmoid colon with adequate mesosigmoid length to reach the anterior abdominal wall without tension.
If the sigmoid is tethered or diseased, a transverse loop colostomy in the right upper quadrant is selected instead.

blocks.title: Key operative steps in outline
bullets: Circular 3 cm cutaneous disc excised at the pre-marked site in the left iliac fossa.
Subcutaneous fat cleared; anterior rectus sheath incised crosswise; rectus abdominis muscle split bluntly along its fibres.
Posterior rectus sheath and peritoneum opened to create a trephine admitting two to three fingerbreadths snugly.
Mobile loop of sigmoid colon identified and delivered through the trephine without axial torsion or mesenteric ischemia.
Plastic bridge, rod, or rubber catheter passed through a small window in the mesosigmoid beneath the bowel loop to support it on the skin.
Transverse incision made along the antimesenteric border across two-thirds of the bowel circumference.
Colonic wall sutured to the skin margins with interrupted 3-0 absorbable sutures; unlike an ileostomy, a colostomy is matured flush with skin.
Stoma bridge left in position for 5 to 7 days until firm peritoneal and fascial adhesions secure the loop to the abdominal wall.

blocks.title: Complications and differences from ileostomy
bullets: Stoma is matured flush with skin because colonic effluent is solid or semi-formed and non-corrosive, unlike caustic liquid ileal output.
Complications: stoma ischaemia from tight trephine or excessive mesenteric traction, retraction, parastomal hernia, and prolapse.
Colostomy prolapse predominantly affects the distal non-functioning limb due to mobile distal bowel sliding through.

viva.q: Why is a colostomy matured flush with the abdominal skin whereas an ileostomy requires a 2 to 3 cm spout?
viva.a: Colonic discharge consists of formed or semi-solid stool devoid of active digestive enzymes, whereas liquid ileal effluent contains destructive proteolytic enzymes that macerate skin.

viva.q: What is the function of the plastic stoma bridge in a loop colostomy, and when is it safely removed?
viva.a: It supports the exteriorised colon above skin level to prevent retraction until fibrous adhesions anchor the bowel, usually removed after 5 to 7 days.

viva.q: How do you distinguish the proximal active limb from the distal non-functioning limb in a loop colostomy?
viva.a: By inspecting peristaltic discharge of faecal matter from the proximal limb and tracing the anatomical mesenteric orientation within the peritoneal cavity.

image.brief: Operative view of a matured loop sigmoid colostomy in the left lower quadrant resting on a white plastic stoma bridge with edges sutured flush to the surrounding skin.
